model.comments: High effort Claude Fable 5.1. Thinking is always on for Fable; depth is controlled by Anthropic's output_config.effort, which OpenRouter sets from reasoning.effort (its verbosity field maps to the same native field, so this equals the older opus-4.x verbosity convention).

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Pentago on a standard 6x6 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(you, opponent) -> str: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - The board is 6x6. - You are given two 6x6 arrays (or array-like objects) containing only 0/1 integers. - `you[r][c] == 1` means your marble is at row `r`, col `c`. - `opponent[r][c] == 1` means the opponent marble is at row `r`, col `c`. - An empty cell means `you[r][c] == 0` and `opponent[r][c] == 0`. - Positions are valid (no overlaps): never `you[r][c] == opponent[r][c] == 1`. - Quadrants are 3x3 sub-boards indexed as: - `quad = 0`: rows 1..3, cols 1..3 (top-left). - `quad = 1`: rows 1..3, cols 4..6 (top-right). - `quad = 2`: rows 4..6, cols 1..3 (bottom-left). - `quad = 3`: rows 4..6, cols 4..6 (bottom-right). - A quadrant rotation rotates the chosen 3x3 sub-board in place and affects BOTH players' marbles in that quadrant. - `L` is 90 degrees anticlockwise; `R` is 90 degrees clockwise. - After placement and rotation, a player wins if they have 5 (or more) marbles in a row in any straight line: horizontal, vertical, or diagonal (either diagonal direction). - If both players have a 5-in-a-row after your move is applied, the result is a draw. - If neither player has a 5-in-a-row and the board is full, the result is a draw. # Action / Return Format - Return a single string move formatted exactly as: `"row,col,quad,dir"`. - `row` is 1..6 (1-indexed). - `col` is 1..6 (1-indexed). - `quad` is 0..3. - `dir` is `L` or `R`. - A legal move must place exactly one of your marbles on an empty cell, then rotate exactly one quadrant 90 degrees in the chosen direction. - Example syntax: `"6,5,2,L"` means place at row 6 col 5, then rotate quadrant 2 left. - You may assume at least one empty cell exists (i.e., `policy` is not called when no legal move exists). # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I need to design a strong Pentago policy that runs within a tight time limit, considering the branching factor of up to 288 possible moves (36 placements times 8 rotations). I'm planning a layered approach: first check for immediate wins, then check for moves that block the opponent's immediate winning replies, before falling back to deeper search with evaluation.

For the evaluation function, I'm counting the 32 distinct five-in-a-row winning lines on the board (12 horizontal, 12 vertical, and 8 diagonal windows) and scoring positions based on how many marbles each player controls per line. To keep things fast in Python, I want to use bitboard representations for the 36 cells along with precomputed rotation lookup tables so quadrant rotations become simple table lookups rather than expensive loops, and I'm weighing whether a full two-ply minimax with alpha-beta pruning is feasible given the 288×288 branching factor.

Given the raw computation cost is likely too slow at ~8M operations per move, I'm thinking about optimizations: deduplicating moves that produce identical resulting boards (since rotating symmetric or near-empty quadrants can yield the same state), sorting moves by a quick static evaluation before doing the deeper search to make alpha-beta cutoffs more effective, and using iterative deepening with a hard time limit so I always have a best move ready even if deeper search doesn't finish. I'm also considering adding a transposition table to avoid recomputing repeated positions.

For the evaluation itself, I'm working out an efficient bitboard approach: for each of the 32 possible winning lines, check whether the line is occupied solely by one player and score it based on how many marbles they have on it using a popcount lookup. I'm also thinking through the tactical nuance that a four-in-a-row threat isn't automatically a forced win, since the rotation requirement after placing means the opponent might be able to disrupt the line depending on which quadrants the line spans.

For move generation, I'm settling on representing state as (me, opp) bitboards, then enumerating all empty-cell placements combined with all 8 possible quadrant rotations, deduplicating resulting positions, and checking for wins after rotation (with simultaneous wins counting as a draw).

For rotation itself, since quadrant bits aren't contiguous in the 6x6 layout, I'm precomputing lookup tables per quadrant and direction that map the 9-bit extracted pattern directly to its rotated version, so rotation becomes a fast mask-and-lookup operation rather than bit-shuffling on the fly.

Now I'm working out evaluation scoring, using weighted counts for line lengths (with 5-in-a-row treated as an immediate win) across all 32 line masks, computed efficiently by iterating over the mask pairs.

Timing-wise this eval loop at ~15µs per call means a full 288×288 move matrix costs over a second, so I need alpha-beta pruning, move ordering, and deduplication to make depth 2 practical, with iterative deepening and per-node time checks handling deeper searches opportunistically. I'm also considering ways to cut branching factor, like collapsing duplicate rotation results and estimating that mid-game there are roughly 20 empty cells times 8 orientations, giving about 160 candidate moves — plus exploring a cheaper one-ply heuristic as an alternative.

Sketching the negamax function now: it counts nodes and checks a time budget periodically, generates and dedupes moves, and evaluates each resulting position for terminal win/loss/draw conditions before recursing with flipped bounds, assigning scores that favor faster wins and treat simultaneous wins as draws.

Working out move ordering...

Actually, I realize win detection can be done with fast bitmask shifts instead—checking horizontal, vertical, and both diagonal runs of five using shifted AND operations against precomputed masks for valid starting positions, each check reducing to just a handful of bitwise ops, so win checks become nearly free (~1µs).

For evaluation though, counting windows with exactly k of my marbles and zero opponent marbles is trickier to bit-parallelize; I could compute opponent-free window masks via shifted ANDs of the complement, but tallying counts of 1-4 within those windows would need bit-sliced adders, which gets complicated. A simpler fallback is just looping over precomputed line masks directly, checking each line's marble counts with straightforward conditionals—slower at roughly 15µs but much easier to implement correctly.

Estimating cost: using popcount per line for ~32 lines lands around 20µs, which feels borderline. I'm also considering restructuring around 18 lines instead of 32 windows—six rows, six columns, and six diagonals of length 5 or more—which could simplify the line-based approach.

Row extraction from bitboards is cheap via simple shifting, but columns and diagonals need a different trick, so I'm exploring precomputed 64-entry lookup tables that map masked bitboard segments to compact 6-bit values, letting me score each line through table lookups rather than recomputation.

With that, 18 lines at ~0.5µs each lands around 9-12µs, so 83k evals take roughly a second — depth-2 full search is borderline without pruning, though alpha-beta with good ordering cuts that substantially. I'm now considering numpy vectorization instead: batch-evaluating all 288 children at once via fancy-indexed lookup tables could drop per-node cost from milliseconds to ~100µs, making depth-2 full search feasible in ~30ms and opening the door to deeper search.

For the bitboard rotation lookup, I'm working out a compact bit-extraction scheme to compress each 9-bit quadrant into an index for array lookup, combining shifted bit groups instead of relying on dict-based masks.

I'm now weighing whether a full numpy-vectorized pipeline is worth it versus keeping the compact-index approach in pure Python, since the operation counts end up comparable.

For the vectorized version, since only my placements vary while the opponent's board stays fixed, I only need to rotate my placements across all 8 rotations while the opponent's rotated boards can be computed once as scalars. Win checks and line-based evaluation would then need vectorized extraction across rows and columns, though columns require a strided bit-compression step that's trickier to vectorize efficiently.

Estimating the cost: roughly 400µs per node to evaluate all children, which puts a full depth-2 search around 115ms but depth-3 balloons to tens of seconds unless alpha-beta pruning cuts it down substantially — still likely too slow for full depth 3 without further optimization.

Comparing against pure Python (~10µs per eval), which is actually faster per-node than the numpy approach at this small scale, giving roughly a 7x speedup and making full depth-2 search feasible in under a second, with alpha-beta pruning bringing it closer to 300ms and pushing partially into depth 3.

I'm weighing whether depth 3 actually matters: depth 2 catches immediate wins and blocks opponent's immediate threats, while depth 3 would let me spot forced wins via double threats, and depth 4 would catch the opponent's double threats — so a threat-counting evaluation function could approximate deeper search without the full cost.

At a depth-2 leaf where it's my turn to move, if I already have an open four-in-a-row threat, that's essentially a win since I get to place the winning piece immediately — so I'm working out how to cheaply detect "I have a winning move available" by checking for windows with four of my pieces and one empty slot, though I need to confirm this detection still holds up after board rotations.

Similarly, opponent open-fours (when it's not their turn) represent unblockable threats I need to weight heavily but below an actual loss, and if they have two simultaneous threats needing different response cells I'm likely already lost. For the line-based evaluation table, I'm sketching weights per window based on count of my pieces versus opponent's — four of mine with zero opponent pieces gets a large score, though rotations complicate how these windows shift.

Rotations disrupt static evaluation significantly in Pentago, so search depth matters more than eval precision. I'm leaning toward numpy-vectorized child evaluation combined with alpha-beta iterative deepening driven by Python recursion — depth-1 leaf nodes compute all child evals vectorized and just take the max, while deeper nodes recurse in a Python loop over children, meaning a depth-2 search costs roughly 288 children times one vectorized eval each, and depth-3 multiplies that further.

Full alpha-beta pruning doesn't really help inside a vectorized leaf node since it evaluates everything at once, but it can prune at the ply-1 level after finding a refutation — though with 288 children per node, even decent move ordering leaves depth-3 search around 3.5 seconds, which is too slow. Restricting the root to the top-K candidates (say K=20) from a depth-2 pass cuts that down to roughly 400ms, which seems much more workable.

Now I'm reconsidering whether the 0.4ms per-node estimate is accurate, and thinking about optimizing the vectorized evaluation itself using precomputed lookup tables on compact bit indices — extracting row and column patterns efficiently via bit shifts and masks for both players across all 18 lines.

I need to check whether this multiplication approach creates collisions between the shifted bits landing in the target region 30-35, since cross terms from different k,j pairs could overlap and corrupt the result.

Checking the algebra confirms no exponent collisions, so no carries occur across columns, meaning I can safely extract each compact column via shift-and-mask-multiply operations without overflow since the max bit position stays within 60, well under uint64 limits. Now I'm thinking about how to extract the diagonal bits for the next step.

Max exponent hits 65, overflowing uint64, but since there are no carries between these distinct bit positions the wraparound just discards high bits without corrupting the target range. Now I'm working out the anti-diagonal case (bits 5,10,15,20,25,30 with stride 5), computing the gather shift 30-4k and the multiplier sum needed.

Checking cross terms for collisions: I find that (k=4,j=5) and (k=0,j=0) both map to exponent 30 regardless of the offset t, so this multiplier choice always corrupts due to overlapping bits. I'm now trying a reversed ordering, mapping bit 5k to position t+5-k with shift t+5-6k, to see if that avoids the collision.

Let me recheck the indexing: bit 5k times multiplier term j lands at position 5k+t+5-6j, and I need this to fall in the target window [t, t+5]. Working through each k value, only j=k satisfies the constraint, confirming no unwanted overlaps occur between terms.

Setting t=25 gives exponents 30,24,18,12,6,0 for the multiplier, matching the diagonal case, and the max exponent stays well within range at 55. Since bit ordering reversal doesn't actually matter here, I'll just build the tables directly by enumerating cells and using a consistent compaction index scheme.

I'm working out the anti-diagonal cell-to-bit mapping: cell (r, 5-r) maps to bit 5r+5, giving bits 5,10,15,20,25,30 for r=0..5.

Now I'm mapping the four shorter length-5 diagonals to their bit positions with strides of 5 or 7, then figuring out how to shift each into alignment with the main pattern for the extraction logic.

I'm also weighing a simpler pure-Python approach: instead of vectorized bit tricks, use dictionary lookups per line keyed by a combined encoding of my bits and opponent bits within the mask, trading some overhead for clarity.

Estimating throughput, pure Python evaluation lands around 10µs per position while numpy vectorization could get 5-8x faster once amortized over batches of children, which matters a lot given how much depth affects search quality. I'm leaning toward the vectorized route despite the added complexity, but I want to be careful about correctness given the risk of subtle bugs, and I'm still considering whether table lookups per node could simplify things further.

Writing vectorized eval logic...

I'll use separate boolean win-flag tables per player rather than relying on a single score encoding, keeping the win detection unambiguous even across different lines.

For generating child boards, I'm working out the gather-heavy approach: building placements, applying all 8 rotations via permutation indexing, then batching the line-window gathers across up to 288 candidate boards to estimate the per-node cost.

For representing placements efficiently, I'm considering initializing each child board via a repeat-then-index-assign pattern rather than tile-plus-set, so each empty cell gets the current player's mark directly without extra copies.

Actually, I decide to keep boards in mover-relative encoding: 1 = current mover, 2 = opponent, and swap the values when passing to the child so perspective flips automatically. Evaluation then always treats "1" as the side to move when scoring lines through the lookup table.

For the scoring logic, I score each 5-length window: pure runs of 1's give positive weight, pure runs of 2's give negative weight, mixed windows score zero, and full runs of five flag a win either way. I'm weighting a four-in-a-row heavily, since after the mover's turn it becomes the opponent's move -- an open four for the opponent should score as a near-loss, while an open four for the mover (that the opponent hasn't yet blocked) should score as a strong but not absolute advantage, since rotations could still disrupt it.

This asymmetry is fine because negamax always evaluates a leaf relative to whoever just moved, so the perspective flips consistently as depth increases. I still need to handle the case where the board fills up completely, resulting in a draw.

Now I'm designing the search function itself: it expands children, computes static evaluations from the mover's view, checks terminal states with win/loss/draw scoring, then orders children by static value and recursively explores them with alpha-beta pruning.

I'm also thinking about deduplicating equivalent child boards efficiently -- rather than a slow full row-uniqueness check, I could hash each board by dotting with a random vector and deduping on hashes instead. This matters most early in the game, since rotating or reflecting empty quadrants often produces identical boards.

I realize an exact deduplication is feasible too: since the board has 36 cells, encoding it in base-3 fits comfortably within a 64-bit integer, giving an exact key with no collision risk instead of relying on probabilistic hashing.

That same key can double as a transposition table entry, storing depth, value, and a flag for exact/lower/upper bounds—useful since rotations create many transpositions from different move orders reaching identical positions. For time management, I'll check elapsed time during expansion and raise a timeout to fall back on the last completed depth's best move, always letting the shallow first depth finish quickly.

With deeper searches, using partial results is trickier: I could fall back to the completed depth's answer, but if a partial search already found a forced win, that should take priority regardless of completeness—otherwise, sticking with the last fully completed depth keeps things safe and simple.

So the update rule: take the current iteration's best move if its first candidate finished searching (since it's ordered from the prior best), otherwise fall back to the previous iteration's move. There's some imprecision since not-yet-searched moves at the new depth could theoretically be better, but that's standard accepted practice.

At the root, I also need to make sure depth ≥ 2 catches immediate losing moves. Now I'm estimating timing budgets: depth-2 search fits in roughly 150ms, leaving about 650ms for a partial depth-3 pass, and I'm working through the branching factor and per-node cost to see how far that gets with alpha-beta pruning at the first ply.

Given the estimated per-node costs, full depth-3 across all root moves looks too slow — likely only the top 30-50% of ordered root moves get depth-3 treatment before time runs out, which is an acceptable tradeoff. I'm considering ways to cut per-node cost, like deduplicating children early in the game or streamlining the expand step so it just needs the max over child values.

Skipping the dedupe brings depth-1 nodes down to roughly 250µs, and win checks could reuse the same table lookup. I consider trying to vectorize a full 2-ply subtree at once, but the numbers blow up fast: 83k boards times line gathers would take tens of milliseconds per node, and scaling that to depth 3 across all root children would take nearly 30 seconds, so going one level deeper vectorized isn't worth it.

I could try forward pruning at ply-1, only considering the top-M opponent replies by static eval plus forced wins, but rotations make ordering unreliable in Pentago. Given the arena likely has random, greedy, and simple minimax opponents, a solid depth-2 search with good eval plus partial depth-3 and tactical checks should perform well enough.

For the eval weights, I'm working through the asymmetry between mover and opponent-to-move windows — treating open-4s as near-certain wins since the opponent can always place their marble and rotate a quadrant not touching that window, guaranteeing the win.

I'm debating whether to score O[4] as an actual WIN value or just a very large heuristic number (like 20000) that dominates other terms but stays below the true WIN score reserved for confirmed wins found in search.

For M[4], the mover's own threat, I want a moderate value since the opponent can still respond, and two simultaneous threats in different cells should roughly double that value to reflect a likely forced win. I'm also weighing whether to add a small positional bonus for quadrant-center cells, since those are more valuable in Pentago due to rotation flexibility, though I want to keep this bonus cheap to compute alongside the rest of the evaluation.

For the transposition table key, I'm hashing the board into a base-3 encoded int64, verifying the maximum value stays safely within int64 range. Now I'm setting up the line indices for rows, columns, and diagonals, padding the shorter diagonals with a dummy always-empty cell so all lines have uniform length, while making sure the lookup table only considers the real window for those shorter lines and not the padded dummy cell.

For the precomputed scoring table, I'm iterating over all possible base-3 digit combinations per line, extracting the 5-cell windows, counting marbles of each color, and assigning score contributions or win flags depending on whether one color dominates a window or a full five-in-a-row is achieved. I'm also working out the rotation permutations for each quadrant, mapping old cell positions to new ones under a clockwise turn.

Move string format combines the row, column, quadrant, and direction into a single move label. Now I'm writing the expand function that generates child boards from quadrant rotations...

Still writing expand logic...

Simplifying positional scoring with a per-cell lookup table gathered by cell value, then computing terminal outcomes: draw if both win, win/loss value if one side wins, otherwise the positional score, plus checking for a full board draw case.

I want faster wins prioritized by subtracting ply from the win value, and I'm planning deduplication via a matmul-based key hash and np.unique, skipping it at depth 1. Now I'm sketching the recursive search function, handling terminal expansion, dedup toggling by depth, and returning max value directly at depth 1.

I'm ordering children by static value descending so wins get explored first, then doing alpha-beta with negamax recursion, updating alpha and pruning when it meets or exceeds beta. I need to fix the sign convention for win values propagated through negation at deeper plies, so terminal wins get WIN minus ply for the mover and the negative for the opponent. I'm also starting to sketch a transposition table lookup at the top of the search function, keyed by the same matmul hash.

Now I'm working through the TT flag logic for exact, lower, and upper bound entries, then moving to the root policy function which builds the board, expands children, checks for immediate wins, and begins iterative deepening ordering moves by prior iteration values.

Continuing the search loop, catching timeouts and falling back to the best move found so far. I also need to handle edge cases like avoiding self-inflicted losing rotations at the root and picking a fallback move when no safe option exists, plus tuning the time budget against the 1-second arena limit.

Setting up permutation and swap arrays with numpy int8 boards to efficiently represent rotations and piece swaps...

Duplicate moves from symmetric quadrant rotations are fine since dedup just picks one. I also need to double check the eval function correctly handles cases where the mover already has an open-four threat versus the opponent, ensuring the win condition triggers properly at leaf nodes.

At depth-2, I'm checking whether the search actually catches the "opponent creates a double threat" defense — if the opponent gets two open fours after my move, I lose regardless of my reply, but the current eval scoring (200 vs 100) treats this as just a magnitude difference rather than a hard loss, so I might need to make the threat count nonlinear to force proper avoidance.

Given the risk of overcounting shared cells, I'll accept the imprecision and just apply a moderate double-threat bonus (+600) while keeping the base open-4 score at 150. I'll mirror this for the opponent's open-4 at leaf nodes, giving it a heavy -20000 penalty since that's essentially a loss.

For depth-1 leaves, I'm just taking the max over children values from the mover's perspective. Estimating performance, depth-2 search at the root would take about 90ms with ~288 leaf expansions at roughly 300µs each, while depth-3 would multiply that further across the root's children.

I'm working through whether we'd realistically get through 10-40 root moves at depth 3 within 600ms, which would still meaningfully improve candidate ranking. One optimization I'm considering: since WIN values are ordered first and alpha-beta cutoffs trigger on v ≥ beta, terminal wins at ply-1 nodes should already short-circuit automatically without needing an extra explicit check.

But full depth 3 is too slow even with forward pruning limited to top candidates by static eval — the numbers don't work out. So partial depth 3 is the fallback. For the root's first move specifically, since alpha starts at -infinity, none of the opponent's replies get pruned, meaning all roughly 288 replies must be fully searched before any cutoff can occur.

Depth-1 results from earlier iterations aren't deep enough to reuse, and transpositions among ply-1 nodes are already deduped at the root, so TT gains would be minimal for shallow searches. Deeper searches only really kick in during the late endgame with few empties, where the branching naturally shrinks — so I'll skip TT altogether for simplicity.

For terminal handling, when only one empty cell remains, all children are full-board terminal states resolving to wins or draws. I need to mark full boards as terminal and think through a positional value heuristic for Pentago: quadrant centers stay fixed under rotation making them stable anchor points, while corner and edge cells cycle through four positions each rotation, and the four central board cells act as quadrant corners with their own strategic weight.

I'm settling on giving centers +3, the central 2x2 cluster +2, and other cells +1 or 0, then implementing this with the line-generation code covering rows, columns, and the various diagonal segments across the 6x6 board, including the shorter length-5 diagonals.

Writing diagonal line code...

Now I'm setting up scoring tables that track open-3 and open-4 window counts per line, along with weight arrays for mover versus opponent threats — giving mover weights like [0,1,4,15,150,0] and opponent weights slightly favoring the next-to-move side since they get to respond first.

Writing board expansion code...

Still writing scoring logic...

Continuing the recursion: at the base depth it returns the max child value, otherwise it sorts children by value descending, recurses with negated bounds, and prunes once alpha meets or exceeds beta. I'm confirming that terminal children (draws etc.) are handled correctly at depth-1 by just taking the max, and that timing checks after each expand call are frequent enough given expand's low cost. With the initial values as a starting point, I'm implementing iterative deepening: at each depth, I loop over children in the current best order, run negated recursive search on terminal-swapped boards to get scores, track the best value and index, and update alpha for pruning as I go, while wrapping everything in a try/except to gracefully fall back to the best move found so far if the search times out mid-iteration.

After each completed depth I re-sort the move order by descending score to improve pruning next iteration, and I check whether the best value is already provably winning or losing within reach to stop early, capping iterations at a max depth. I also confirm the negamax sign convention is correct — passing negated alpha/beta bounds to child search so that fail-soft cutoffs still produce valid, if approximate, upper-bound scores for move ordering purposes.

I should double check timing feasibility for depth-2 to reliably complete, though even if it doesn't finish, falling back to depth-1's best ordering still avoids obvious blunders.

Actually the depth-1 eval already captures opponent open-4 threats via the penalty term, so it correctly avoids leaving those. At depth-2, the perspective flips correctly too — my open 4 after their reply still shows as a win for me, which checks out logically.

Now I'm verifying the swap array shape and moving on to estimate the numpy overhead for the expand step at n=30, roughly tallying microsecond costs for flatnonzero, repeat, fancy indexing, and the permutation lookups.

I'm working through how to compute the line index encoding efficiently — comparing a batched matmul against an explicit sum-of-powers-of-three approach across the 3D arrays, weighing whether integer dtype forces generic loop execution instead of BLAS, and considering switching to float32 for speed.

Tallying up the remaining gather and reduction steps for scoring, cell values, and dedup — each costing roughly 5-30µs — the total lands around 250-300µs, matching my earlier estimate.

I wonder if I can pack score, win1, win2, and t4 into a single int64 field per line to combine the gather/sum operations, but bit budgeting is tricky: summing across 18 lines means each field needs enough headroom to avoid overflow bleeding into adjacent bits, so the score field alone would need ~26 bits with an offset to stay non-negative.

Rechecking the bit budget, win1 fits at bit 30 (6 bits: 30-35), win2 at 36-41, t4 at 42-47, then decoding pulls the score out of the lower bits while shifting to extract each flag from the packed sum. I'm also thinking about whether the positional cell value could fold directly into the row-line table, since each cell belongs to exactly one row line, letting me avoid a separate gather.

For each row line, I'm adding cell bonuses from the position table based on whether the digit is 1 or 2, at no extra cost, so the per-child evaluation becomes just a gather, sum, and decode. Now I need to double check the rotation permutation math against the arena's semantics for rotating a chosen 3x3 sub-board anticlockwise, verifying my index mapping matches the standard row-1-at-top, col-1-at-left viewing convention.

Working through a concrete 3x3 example, I confirm clockwise rotation maps new(i,j) to old(2-j,i), and anticlockwise maps new(i,j) to old(j,2-i), both checking out against manual rotation of a sample grid. I also verify the numpy fancy-indexing convention translates correctly into the inverse permutation needed for the clockwise case.

I'm precomputing powers of 3 for encoding board states, capping input arrays to int64 and converting any list-like inputs into properly shaped 6x6 numpy arrays with nonzero masking. I'm also setting a depth cap tied to the number of empty cells so the search naturally bottoms out at terminal positions rather than running indefinitely.

For terminal detection, when a board fills up completely I mark it as terminal with a draw value of zero unless a win condition triggers, ensuring the search never recurses into a fully occupied board. I'm also setting a 0.7-second time budget with some margin for root overhead to keep total runtime safely under 0.8 seconds.

I'm bumping WIN to 10^7 and INF to 10^9 to keep clear separation from eval magnitudes. I'm reasoning through the ply-dependent win values — since scores negate at each level, faster wins should still score higher at the root, and checking through an example confirms the win-in-3-plies case scores correctly as WIN-2.
